title: Mastering the Pause: Compassion and Positive Intent
author: Heather McGonigal
summary: In the closing episode of her four-part Power of the Pause series, executive coach Heather McGonigal argues that assuming positive intent is not naive optimism but a specific leadership discipline: pausing before deciding what someone else's behavior means, rather than letting the mind fill an information gap with the worst possible story. She grounds this in an asymmetry every leader has lived, when we mess up we know our own good intentions and full context, but when someone else's mistake affects us we lack that internal access and default to hostile interpretations like "they clearly do not care." McGonigal is explicit that assuming positive intent does not mean ignoring real problems, abandoning boundaries, or skipping accountability; it means creating enough space to ask what might actually be true before reacting. The piece closes the series by reframing its whole premise: the pause was never really about becoming calmer, but about reclaiming the leader's power to choose how to show up regardless of how others behave.
points: McGonigal names a specific cognitive asymmetry: when we ourselves fall short we have full context and know our intent, but when someone else's mistake affects us we lack that access and the brain fills the gap with the worst-case story.

She draws an explicit boundary around the practice: assuming positive intent does not mean ignoring difficult behavior, abandoning accountability, or excusing real problems — it is a starting posture for inquiry, not a conclusion.

The four discussion questions she offers (What happened here? What might I not know? What needs to change? What conversation or boundary would help next time?) turn compassion into an operational leadership tool rather than a feeling.

The series' final reframe is significant: the Power of the Pause was never primarily about becoming calmer, but about preserving a leader's power to choose their own response regardless of how the other person behaved.
quotes: Do your best to assume positive intent as your default setting. Not because everyone always gets it right. Not because difficult behavior should be ignored. And not because compassion means abandoning boundaries or accountability.

We know that we were doing the best we could at that moment. But when someone else's mistake impacts us, we do not have access to their internal experience. And our brains can quickly fill that gap with the worst possible interpretation.
But when we get completely hooked by those stories, it becomes much harder to see what might improve the situation. Compassion can give us enough freedom to look again.

My hope is that you take away from this series that the Power of the Pause is not simply about becoming calmer. It is about creating enough space to choose how you want to think, respond, and show up, even when other people do not behave exactly as you hoped they would.
You do not have to excuse everything. You do not have to agree with everything. But you can practice giving yourself and others a little more grace.
